cards.definition: Data definition language: the statements that define or change the structure of the database.
cards.useCase: CREATE, ALTER and DROP are DDL. In MySQL they end the current transaction.

cards.definition: Builds a new table with its columns, data types and constraints.
cards.useCase: Use it to define a table that does not exist yet.

cards.definition: Adds a new column to an existing table. Existing rows get NULL, or the DEFAULT.
cards.useCase: Use it when a table needs one more attribute.
cards.example: ALTER TABLE member ADD COLUMN phone VARCHAR(20);

cards.definition: Changes the definition of an existing column. It restates the whole definition.
cards.useCase: Use it to change a type or size; repeat NOT NULL and DEFAULT to keep them.
cards.example: ALTER TABLE book MODIFY COLUMN title VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL;

cards.definition: The value a column takes when an INSERT leaves it out.
cards.useCase: Use it for a sensible starting value such as a status.

cards.definition: A rule the database enforces on every insert and update; a row that breaks it is rejected.
cards.useCase: Use them to keep bad data out whichever application writes it.
cards.example: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, PRIMARY KEY

cards.definition: A constraint that requires a value in the column.
cards.useCase: Use it for facts every row must have.

cards.definition: A constraint that stops two rows sharing a value in the column. NULLs are allowed.
cards.useCase: Use it for values that identify a row but are not the primary key, such as an email.

cards.definition: A constraint that rejects a row when a condition on its values is false. Enforced from MySQL 8.0.16.
cards.useCase: Use it for ranges and simple rules; a NULL passes, so add NOT NULL too.

cards.definition: Adds a named constraint to an existing table with ALTER TABLE.
cards.useCase: Use it to add a rule after the table is built.
cards.example: ALTER TABLE member ADD CONSTRAINT uq_email UNIQUE (email);

cards.definition: Data manipulation language: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, the statements that change rows.
cards.useCase: Use them to add, change and remove data; the table structure stays the same.

cards.definition: Adds one or more rows. Name the columns, or supply a value for every column in order.
cards.useCase: Columns left out take their DEFAULT or NULL.

cards.definition: Changes values in existing rows: SET gives the new values, WHERE picks the rows.
cards.useCase: No WHERE means every row is changed.
cards.example: UPDATE item SET price = 9.99 WHERE item_id = 12;

cards.definition: Removes rows that match the WHERE condition. With no WHERE it removes every row but keeps the table.
cards.useCase: To remove the table itself use DROP TABLE.

cards.definition: Removes a table completely: its structure and all of its rows.
cards.useCase: Use it when the table is no longer needed.

cards.definition: A group of statements treated as one unit: all of it takes effect, or none of it.
cards.useCase: Use it when several changes must succeed together, such as a transfer.
cards.example: Subtract 100 from A and add 100 to B

cards.definition: Opens a transaction; changes stay provisional until COMMIT or ROLLBACK.
cards.useCase: Start one before a group of related changes.

cards.definition: Makes all the changes of the current transaction permanent.
cards.useCase: Run it when every step has succeeded; a ROLLBACK cannot undo it afterwards.

cards.definition: Undoes all the changes made since the transaction began.
cards.useCase: Run it when a step fails, to restore the starting state.

cards.definition: MySQL's default: each statement commits on its own unless a transaction was started.
cards.useCase: START TRANSACTION switches it off until COMMIT or ROLLBACK.
cards.example: A lone UPDATE is saved immediately

cards.definition: Atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability: the properties of a reliable transaction.
cards.useCase: Atomic is all or nothing; durable means committed work survives a crash.

cards.definition: A structure that lets the database find rows by a column's value without reading the whole table.
cards.useCase: Speeds up reads; slows writes and uses storage. It does not change results.
cards.example: Like the index of a book

cards.definition: A balanced, sorted tree: the default index type, good for equality, ranges and ORDER BY.
cards.useCase: Use it for most columns.

cards.definition: An index that jumps to an exact value. It handles equality only, not ranges.
cards.useCase: Used by the MEMORY engine for exact lookups.

cards.definition: Builds an index on one or more columns: CREATE INDEX name ON table (column).
cards.useCase: Index columns used often in WHERE and JOIN that have many different values.

cards.definition: Removes an index: DROP INDEX name ON table.
cards.useCase: Drop indexes nobody uses, since they slow writes.

cards.definition: An index on two or more columns together, used from its leftmost column on.
cards.useCase: A filter on the first column can use it; a filter on only the second cannot.
cards.example: CREATE INDEX idx_name ON person (last_name, first_name);

cards.definition: A prefix for SELECT that shows the execution plan: which index is used and how many rows are examined.
cards.useCase: Use it to find out why a query is slow. It does not return the rows.
cards.example: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM member WHERE email = 'a@x.com';

cards.definition: MySQL reads every row of the table to answer the query.
cards.useCase: A warning sign on a big table; an index on the filtered column may help.

cards.definition: possible_keys lists indexes that could be used; key is the one actually chosen (NULL if none).
cards.useCase: Check key after adding an index to see that it is used.

cards.definition: A condition that cannot use an index on the column, such as a function on the column or a leading wildcard.
cards.useCase: Rewrite as a range on the plain column, or a LIKE that begins with fixed text.

cards.definition: A mechanism that stops users working at the same time from corrupting each other's data.
cards.useCase: Released when the transaction ends with COMMIT or ROLLBACK.
cards.example: An UPDATE locks the row it changes

cards.definition: A lock on a whole table: others wait to write any row.
cards.useCase: Simple and cheap, but limits concurrency.

cards.definition: A lock on only the rows a statement touches, so other rows stay available.
cards.useCase: InnoDB uses it, so many users can update one table at once.
cards.example: SELECT * FROM seat WHERE seat_id = 5 FOR UPDATE;

cards.definition: A lock on a single value in a single row: the finest granularity.
cards.useCase: Most concurrency but most overhead; a concept, not offered by MySQL.

cards.definition: A shared (read) lock can be held by many users; an exclusive (write) lock by one, blocking all others.
cards.useCase: Readers can share; a writer needs the data to itself.
cards.example: Two readers at once, one writer alone

cards.definition: Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so neither can continue.
cards.useCase: InnoDB detects it and rolls one transaction back. Keep transactions short.
cards.example: A waits for B's row while B waits for A's row
